rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 10 compounds if possible and reveal the occupied phi window and whether any peaks are truncated or unretained. The wide range and moderate slope should give a useful first map of retention and crowding for subsequent optimization.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the only score loss is from t_last = 12.64 min; the next step is to compress the run while keeping peaks inside the gradient. The observed elution window corresponds roughly to phi_e about 0.11 to 0.32, so a trimmed gradient centered on that region with a shorter tG should pull the last peak earlier and test how much time can be removed before the weakest pair starts to suffer.

We still have full resolution credit, so push for a shorter last peak by increasing temperature and slightly steepening the same well-targeted gradient window. This tests whether the critical pair around peaks 6–7 is robust enough to tolerate more compression while moving t_last closer to 10 min.

The critical 6/7 pair collapsed when the method was made hotter and steeper, while all peaks were still comfortably before 10 min. Keep the favorable higher temperature for speed but lengthen tG one step to recover that pair’s resolution without reintroducing a time penalty.

The 6/7 pair is highly temperature-sensitive: raising T to 50 C destroyed its resolution even when tG increased, while the 40 C run was fully resolved. Test an intermediate temperature with the faster 8 min gradient to see if we can keep t_last under 10 min while restoring enough selectivity for that critical pair.

The critical pair worsens mainly with higher temperature, so return to 40 C where all pairs were fully resolved and instead narrow the gradient window to make it shallower without lengthening the run. Since the observed peaks occupy only about phi_e 0.14–0.41 in the successful 10 min run, lowering phi1 should focus gradient time on the crowded region and may keep full resolution while bringing the last peak to about 10 min or less.

The last peak in the 40 C methods is clearly hold-eluting, so narrowing by lowering phi1 was the wrong direction; to reduce t_last we need a stronger end composition while preserving the cooler temperature that keeps the critical pair resolved. Raising both phi0 and phi1 should move the whole pattern earlier, especially the late peak, and tests whether we can get all peaks under 10 min at 40 C without sacrificing the 6/7 pair.

The current method is near-optimal, with only the 6/7 pair slightly below full-credit resolution; that pair should benefit from a slightly shallower gradient while all peaks are already comfortably before 10 min. Lowering phi1 one step keeps the same temperature and start conditions but spends more gradient time in the crowded middle region to try to push R(6,7) above 1.5 without incurring a time penalty.

We already have a perfect CRF, so a sensible final probe is whether the same phi window can be made faster while preserving full resolution. Shortening tG one step tests the margin around the critical 6/7 pair and could reveal whether the optimum is broad or knife-edge.

The 6/7 pair is the only limiter and it improved when the gradient was made slightly shallower at the same temperature, while t_last at the optimum sits right on the 10 min threshold. Lowering phi1 one more step should further improve the critical pair; even if the last peak drifts a little later, there is a good chance it remains effectively at or just under the cutoff.

Injection 10 showed that lowering phi1 improves the critical pair but makes the last peak too late, so the next lever is to raise phi0 to shift the whole profile earlier while keeping the shallower upper window. This could preserve the stronger 6/7 resolution seen at phi1 0.50 and pull t_last back toward 10 min.

A second perfect method is now available, and this variant tests whether a slightly stronger end composition can create more safety margin against the first peak becoming too close to unretained while still keeping the critical 6/7 pair above 1.5. It maps the breadth of the optimum plateau around the current best conditions.

This should make the gradient slightly shallower than the current perfect method, which may increase margin on the critical 6/7 pair while still keeping the last peak under 10 min because raising phi0 already shifted the whole pattern earlier. It directly tests whether injection 11 sits near the center of a broader optimum plateau.

Two perfect methods suggest a narrow ridge where raising phi0 shortens the late peak while lower phi1 preserves the 6/7 pair, so push phi0 one step higher while keeping phi1 at 0.55. This checks whether the optimum can be shifted earlier without losing full-credit resolution, though the first peak is starting to approach the unretained region.

Phi0 = 0.25 pushed the first pair too close to unretained, so stay at the better-balanced phi0 = 0.20 and lengthen the gradient one step to add margin to the critical 6/7 pair. This tests whether injection 11 is just barely perfect or whether a slightly shallower gradient preserves full score with more robustness.

We already have perfect methods at 40 C, so this run is to probe whether a modest temperature increase can maintain full resolution if compensated by a shallower gradient. It tests whether the 6/7 selectivity loss with temperature is partly recoverable by slope, potentially defining a broader operating space around the optimum.

We already know 0.20/0.55/8/40 is perfect; this run checks how much speed margin exists at the same favorable selectivity. If the 6/7 pair stays above 1.5, this would identify a faster equally optimal operating point; if not, it brackets the minimum viable tG around the best method.

The 6/7 pair is the only real limiter and it degrades as temperature rises, so a cooler run may increase selectivity while the current perfect method already has enough time margin below 10 min to absorb some retention increase. This tests whether 35 C gives a more robust fully resolved plateau around the same phi window.

Cooling to 35 C changed selectivity and shifted the critical overlap from 6/7 to 5/6, so the pair is not solved by temperature alone. Lowering phi0 one step at the same phi1 and tG should move those middle peaks to a slightly different part of the gradient and test whether the 35 C selectivity can be rescued by a different phi window.

We have mapped 35 and 50 C and both are worse, but the interaction of temperature with phi0 may matter because 0.20/0.55/8/40 is perfect whereas 0.15/0.55/8/45 was not. Testing 45 C at the better phi window closes that gap and confirms whether the optimum truly sits narrowly at 40 C.

With the maximum CRF already achieved, use the remaining runs to map the edge of the optimum region. Combining the higher phi0 that shortened the late peak with the lower phi1 that helped the 6/7 pair will test whether both effects can coexist, though it may stress the first pair near the dead-time region.

With the optimum already found, this run maps the strong-solvent side boundary from the perfect 0.20/0.55/8/40 method. Increasing phi1 one more step will show how rapidly the critical 6/7 pair deteriorates as the gradient steepens while keeping the safer phi0 that avoids the 1/2 collapse seen at 0.25.

The remaining unknown is whether a small cooling from 40 C can preserve the successful 0.15/0.55/8 phi window while improving the critical 6/7 selectivity without the stronger rearrangement seen at 35 C. This probes the low-temperature boundary near the already perfect 0.15/0.55/8/40 method.

The best score is already secured, so use the final two runs to define another edge of the design space by combining a wider, steeper upper window with a longer gradient at the successful 40 C. This tests whether extra high-end strength plus added slope compensation can still keep the critical mid-pair above full-credit resolution.

The final run should map the corresponding higher-phi0 corner near the newly perfect 0.15/0.65/10/40 method. Since 0.20/0.55/8/40 was also perfect, this tests whether raising both phi0 and phi1 while keeping the longer gradient still preserves full resolution and perhaps offers another robust optimum with an earlier last peak.
